name: Primary generalised glucocorticoid resistance (Chrousos syndrome, NR3C1)

clinicalPearls: Caused by inactivating mutations in NR3C1, the gene for the glucocorticoid receptor, producing generalised tissue insensitivity to cortisol
Compensatory activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis produces high cortisol and ACTH without the physical features of Cushing syndrome
Excess ACTH also drives adrenal steroids with mineralocorticoid and androgenic activity, so hypertension, hypokalaemic alkalosis and androgen excess dominate the picture
Women may have hirsutism, menstrual irregularity and acne; children may show precocious puberty; men may have impaired fertility
Some individuals are asymptomatic and are detected only through family screening
The key paradox is biochemical hypercortisolaemia with loss of normal cortisol feedback but without a Cushingoid phenotype
Cortisol does not suppress normally on dexamethasone testing, reflecting receptor resistance rather than autonomous secretion
Management uses a high-affinity synthetic glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone to suppress ACTH and thereby reduce the excess mineralocorticoid and androgen precursors
reference.pathophysiology: Primary generalised glucocorticoid resistance results from loss-of-function mutations in NR3C1, which encodes the glucocorticoid receptor, reducing the receptor's ligand affinity, nuclear translocation or transactivation. Target tissues therefore respond poorly to cortisol, impairing negative feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary. Compensatory rises in corticotropin-releasing hormone and ACTH increase adrenocortical output; because the excess cortisol cannot act normally there is no Cushingoid phenotype, but the accompanying surge in ACTH-driven steroids with mineralocorticoid activity such as deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, together with adrenal androgens, produces hypertension, hypokalaemic alkalosis and hyperandrogenism. Severity tracks the degree of receptor dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Cushing syndrome from true glucocorticoid excess, which must be excluded
Polycystic ovary syndrome and other causes of hyperandrogenism
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess and other monogenic hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Serum cortisol and plasma ACTH, both elevated, with an upward-shifted but preserved circadian rhythm
24-hour urinary free cortisol, elevated without clinical hypercortisolism
Dexamethasone suppression testing showing resistance to feedback suppression
Serum androgens and steroid precursors with electrolytes and renin/aldosterone
Careful clinical assessment documenting the absence of Cushingoid features
redFlags: Severe hypertension with hypokalaemia risking cardiac and renal complications
Marked androgen excess causing virilisation, or ambiguous genitalia in an affected newborn
Fatigue or hypoglycaemia suggesting inadequate glucocorticoid action at tissue level during stress
reference.prognosis: With appropriate suppression of ACTH using synthetic glucocorticoids, hypertension and androgen excess can be controlled and the prognosis is good; untreated disease risks cardiovascular morbidity and reproductive dysfunction.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the biochemical hypercortisolaemia as Cushing syndrome and pursuing unnecessary adrenal or pituitary surgery
Failing to appreciate that treatment aims to suppress ACTH rather than to replace cortisol
Overlooking milder cases found only on family screening
Attributing hyperandrogenism solely to polycystic ovary syndrome
references: Reviews on the glucocorticoid receptor and glucocorticoid resistance
management: Administer a synthetic glucocorticoid with high glucocorticoid and low mineralocorticoid activity, such as dexamethasone, to suppress the elevated ACTH and thereby reduce the ACTH-driven mineralocorticoid and androgen excess
Control mineralocorticoid-driven hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis, adding a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone or eplerenone if needed
Manage androgen excess such as hirsutism, acne and menstrual irregularity once ACTH is suppressed, and in children treat precocious puberty while monitoring growth
Titrate the glucocorticoid carefully to the lowest effective dose to avoid inducing iatrogenic Cushing syndrome
Monitor plasma ACTH, cortisol, adrenal androgens, electrolytes and blood pressure to guide dose adjustment
Offer genetic counselling and screen first-degree relatives, as inactivating NR3C1 variants are heritable and some carriers are asymptomatic
